Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Fees page: document recording 1-5 pages $105.00 (6-25 amount truncated) (from the parish site listing; confirm with the office)

Fees

Selling in Jefferson Parish?
We buy Jefferson Parish houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Jefferson BOR appeal deadline not found

Is there a Jefferson County clerk of court in Louisiana?

Louisiana has parishes instead of counties, so the office people search for as the Jefferson County clerk of court is the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, based in Gretna. The Clerk's website describes its Mortgage and Conveyance department as the keeper of the parish's official public land records, which is where a house sale ends up on paper.

The Clerk also runs the 24th Judicial District Court records, the First and Second Parish Courts and the Juvenile Court records. For a seller, the land records office is the one that matters on closing day.

Where is Jefferson Parish, and what does that mean for a seller?

Jefferson Parish is a large suburban parish next to New Orleans, split by the Mississippi River into an East Bank and a West Bank. According to Wikipedia, the 2020 census counted 440,781 residents. Gretna is the parish seat, Metairie is the largest community, and Kenner is the largest incorporated city.

The parish measures 665 square miles in total, but only 296 of them are land because Lake Pontchartrain borders the north and much of the southern half is marsh. Grand Isle is reached only by roads that run through Lafourche and St. Charles parishes. The legislature created the parish in 1825 and set its current border with Orleans Parish in 1874, when the parish seat moved to Gretna.

TypePlaces in Jefferson Parish
CitiesGretna (parish seat), Harahan, Kenner, Westwego
TownsGrand Isle, Jean Lafitte
Largest unincorporated communityMetairie
Other named communitiesAvondale, Bridge City, Harvey, Marrero, River Ridge, Terrytown, Waggaman and more

The Clerk's land records sit on the West Bank in Gretna. A seller in Metairie or Kenner who wants to look at records in person has to cross the river, which is one reason the e-recording system described below matters.

Where does the Jefferson Parish clerk record a deed?

Deeds and other real estate documents are recorded by the Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department in the Jefferson Parish General Government Building, 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. The office is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, excluding legal holidays. The mailing address is P.O. Box 10, Gretna, LA 70054-0010.

  • General information on prices and copies: (504) 364-2943 or (504) 364-2944.
  • Certificates and UCC research: (504) 364-2954.
  • Mortgage cancellations: (504) 364-2963.
  • Email: mortgageinfo@jeffparishclerk.gov.

The Clerk lists several kinds of documents it records for the parish: real estate transfers and acts of sale, mortgages, liens and judgments, military discharges, corporation charters, trade name affidavits, and oil, gas and mineral lease transfers. The East Bank office in the Joseph S. Yenni Building handles marriage licenses, passports and elections, and does not list land records among its services.

How soon must a Jefferson Parish act of sale be recorded?

Louisiana law gives a notary 15 days to record a sale of land outside Orleans Parish. Under R.S. 35:199, notaries must record acts of sale, exchange, donation and mortgage of immovable property that pass before them, and for property outside the parish of Orleans they must file with the proper parish recorder within fifteen days.

In practice, a Louisiana sale is signed before a notary at closing, and the title company or the closing attorney sends the act to the Clerk. Because the statute puts the duty on the notary, the closing agent normally handles the filing, and the seller's part is to provide a correct legal description and signed documents.

What does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

Recording a document of 1 to 5 pages costs $105 at the Jefferson Parish Clerk. The Clerk's fee page sets mortgage and conveyance fees under R.S. 13:844 and says the office receives no ad valorem tax funding, so its operations are paid by fees set by the Legislature.

Document recordingFee
1 to 5 pages$105.00
6 to 25 pages$205.00
26 to 50 pages$305.00
51 pages or more$305.00 for the first 50 pages, then $5.00 per page

The base fee covers all parts of the act and its attachments, such as exhibits, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates and surveys. It includes one certified copy and indexing of up to ten names. Further names cost $5.00 each, pages larger than 8.5 by 14 inches add $20.00 per page, and the fee is charged once for each book designation, so a document recorded as both a conveyance and a mortgage costs double.

Since August 1, 2018, every recording also carries a $5.00 fee under R.S. 13:754 that supports the statewide LCRAA system, charged once per instrument.

Is there a transfer tax on a Jefferson Parish sale?

The Clerk's fee schedule shows no transfer tax line. What it lists for a sale is the recording charge, any certificates ordered, and the optional extras that closing agents add. Confirm with your closing attorney or title company, who prepare the settlement statement, since they know what applies to a given deal.

The costs that do appear on the Clerk's page are these:

  • Mortgage or lien and privilege certificate: $20.00 for the first name and $10.00 for each additional name; $40.00 more if clerk staff prepare it.
  • Act or affidavit to cancel a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.00.
  • Release of a mortgage with the original paraphed note: $10.00 per mortgage; a Notice of Cancellation adds $10.00 per mortgage inscription released.
  • Copies: $1.00 per page uncertified, and $10.00 per document certified plus copy costs for mortgage records.

Since April 7, 2017, the Clerk has contracted with Jefferson Certificate Corp. in Gretna to prepare mortgage and conveyance certificates. The Clerk's page gives (504) 361-0206 for ordinary acts of sale or mortgage.

Can I record a Jefferson Parish deed online?

Yes. The Clerk accepts mortgage and conveyance documents, including requests to cancel mortgage inscriptions, through JeffNet, its secure online records system. The system gives 24-hour access to property, civil, criminal and other public records.

JeffNet optionPriceWhat it includes
24-hour access$5.00Online access to records; certified copies at $0.75 per page plus a $10.00 certification fee for mortgage records
Monthly subscription$50.00 per user IDE-filing and e-recording, available to all monthly subscribers and not limited to attorneys

Because e-recording is open to all monthly subscribers, a closing agent can file a sale without a trip to Gretna. A seller can use the 24-hour option to look up the recorded mortgage on the house.

Which Jefferson Parish clerk filings matter to sellers with estate or foreclosure problems?

Two clerk filings commonly come up for sellers who cannot close cleanly: a succession for an inherited house, and executory process, which is Louisiana's foreclosure suit. The civil fee table lists advance deposits for both.

Filing in the 24th JDCAdvance deposit
Succession under $125,000 (La. C.C.P. Art. 3422)$200.00
Succession of $125,000 and over$400.00
Executory process (foreclosure)$1,000.00
Judicial eviction trial in a Parish Court$375.00 plus a bond set by the court

The page calls these a guide and says the actual charge can vary. A succession is the court filing used to settle a deceased owner's estate, which is why it comes up for inherited houses in Gretna, Marrero, Kenner and elsewhere in the parish. The 24th JDC civil records are at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2400, in the same complex as the land records office.

More questions about Jefferson Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

Deeds are recorded by the Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department of the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. It is open weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

The fee is $105.00 for 1 to 5 pages, $205.00 for 6 to 25 pages and $305.00 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5.00 per page beyond 50. A $5.00 LCRAA fee also applies to each recording.

Does the Jefferson Parish Clerk list a transfer tax?

Its fee schedule has no transfer tax line. Ask the closing attorney or title company what appears on your settlement statement.

Can my title company e-record a Jefferson Parish deed?

Yes, through JeffNet. E-recording is available to all monthly subscribers at $50.00 per user ID, not only to attorneys.

How long does a notary have to record a sale in Jefferson Parish?

Fifteen days. R.S. 35:199 requires notaries to record sales of immovable property outside Orleans Parish with the parish recorder within fifteen days after the act is passed.

What do I need to sell an inherited house in Jefferson Parish?

A succession is the court filing for settling a deceased owner's estate. The Clerk lists an advance deposit of $200.00 for a succession under $125,000 and $400.00 for larger ones, and says actual costs may vary.

Lafayette Parish, LA Clerk of Court: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Lafayette Parish, LA Clerk of Court sale

Selling in Lafayette Parish? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Fees

Selling in Lafayette Parish?

What we could not confirm

  • Lafayette BOR appeal deadline not found

What does the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court do with a deed?

The clerk records the deed, which is how a Louisiana property sale becomes effective against everyone outside the contract. Under Civil Code article 3338, a written instrument that transfers an immovable has no effect as to a third person until it is recorded in the conveyance records.

Lafayette Parish's clerk, Louis J. Perret, serves the 15th Judicial District and acts as the ex-officio recorder. The Recording Department files conveyance, mortgage and UCC documents deposited in the parish. When a document is presented, it receives an entry number with the date, hour and minute of filing, and a short description and the first parties appear on the clerk's online records search right away.

The clerk reports that about two to three hundred documents are filed each day, and that full indexing with all party names is complete by the following day.

What are the recording fees for a Lafayette Parish deed?

A conveyance or mortgage of one to five pages costs $105 to record in a single index type. The clerk's schedule includes the $5 statewide portal fee, up to ten names indexed and one certified copy in each price.

Document lengthOne book (conveyance or mortgage)Both books
1 to 5 pages$105$205
6 to 25 pages$205$405
26 to 50 pages$305$605
51 pages or more$305 plus $5 per extra page$605 plus $5 per extra page

The two-book column applies when one document goes into both records, and the fees are assessed separately for each book, except for the single $5 portal charge. The schedule also lists $5 for each name after the tenth, $20 per page for paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and $25 per debtor on a judgment with no Social Security or tax ID number.

Is there a new recording charge coming in 2027?

Yes. The clerk's fee page announces that, effective January 1, 2027, Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document. A closing set for late December 2026 and one set for early January 2027 can therefore carry different recording totals.

The existing $5 portal fee dates from Act 173 of 2017, effective August 1, 2018. It funds the Louisiana Clerks Remote Access Authority, a state entity that runs a statewide portal for remote access to parish land records. Both charges are in addition to the page-based fee, so ask the closing office for the total before the closing date.

What other charges might appear at a Lafayette Parish closing?

Several smaller line items show up around the main recording fee, and the clerk's schedule lists them plainly.

  • Cancellation or partial release of a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.
  • Cancellation with the original paraphed note: $15.
  • Real estate mortgage certificate: $20 for the first name, $10 for each additional name, and $15 for each additional property.
  • Non-lien certificate: $20 per name.
  • Copies: $1 per page in the office, $10 plus the copy fee for a certified copy, and $5 plus the copy fee for a conformed copy.

A mortgage certificate lists the recorded mortgages and privileges that stand against a seller's name. Title agents order it to confirm that every lien is paid and cancelled before the buyer's money is released.

How are documents prepared and submitted in Lafayette Parish?

The clerk wants every document to carry a caption identifying the type of act on its first page, with a 2 inch margin at the top and 1 inch at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than 8 point. Paper can be 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and the clerk cites R.S. 13:844(B) for these rules.

A single document counts as all the pages presented together, including exhibits, riders, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates, surveys and mortgage certificates. That matters for the price, because the page count determines the tier.

Electronic recording is encouraged. The clerk's home page links three e-recording platforms, CSC, ePN and Simplifile, and most title companies already use one of them. If you mail a paper act, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope or the postage is charged at actual cost.

Does the clerk return original documents?

No. The clerk states that, unlike most other states, original documents sent to the Clerk of the District Court and Ex-Officio Recorder are not returned. They become part of the parish archives.

What a filer can get back is a certified copy. It can be requested at the time of filing from the Recording Department, or later from the Land Records and Copy Department. A seller who needs proof of the sale for the Assessor or a lender should order that copy during closing.

Cancellations follow a separate path. They go first to the Cancellation Clerk in the Recording Department for verification, and in Lafayette Parish they must be in authentic form, executed before a notary public and signed by the affiant. UCC terminations use a Louisiana-approved form and can be sent directly.

How can you search Lafayette Parish land records?

The clerk's online records search covers mortgage, conveyance and UCC records, and the free eClerks LA portal indexes land, civil, marriage and probate records across Louisiana. A free alert service on eClerks LA monitors land records across parishes.

Paid land records access, including document images, is sold as a subscription: $20 for one day, $50 for 30 days or $600 for 365 days, with a $1 per page printing fee. Searching the index for liens under a seller's name before listing can show a forgotten mortgage or judgment that would otherwise appear at closing.

The clerk's home page notes that filings may become public record under the Public Records Act, and it lists items prohibited in the courthouse, including cellphones, cameras and recording devices. Bring paper documents and a printed list of the numbers you need rather than relying on a phone.

You can reach the clerk at 800 S. Buchanan St., Lafayette, LA 70501, or by mail at P.O. Box 2009, Lafayette, LA 70502. The main number is (337) 291-6400, and the Recording Department is at (337) 291-6310.

What should a seller confirm before the deed is recorded?

Confirm that property taxes are paid, because Louisiana lets any party to a conveyance of real property outside New Orleans obtain a certificate showing whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes have been paid, other than those for the year of the sale (R.S. 9:2901).

  • Ask for the tax certificate and for a mortgage certificate on every owner's name.
  • Check that any prior mortgage has a cancellation ready to record.
  • Ask the closing office whether the recording date falls before or after January 1, 2027.
  • Request a certified copy of the recorded act for your own file.

A seller who plans to take a cash offer should review the same list, since the buyer's title agent will run these searches before funding. Surprises are easier to fix before the closing day than after.

More questions about Lafayette Parish, LA Clerk of Court

How much does it cost to record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

A one to five page conveyance in a single book costs $105, which includes a $5 portal fee, ten indexed names and one certified copy. Six to 25 pages costs $205.

Is there a transfer tax charge on the Lafayette Parish fee schedule?

The fee schedule we opened lists recording, cancellation, copy and certificate fees but no transfer tax line. Ask your closing agent for the full settlement figures.

Does the Lafayette Parish clerk return my original deed?

No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can obtain a certified copy at filing or later from the Land Records and Copy Department.

Can I e-record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

Yes, and the clerk encourages it. The clerk's site links to CSC, ePN and Simplifile for electronic recording of mortgage, conveyance and UCC documents.

What changes on January 1, 2027?

Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document starting that date, according to the clerk's fee page.

title: Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax
content:
Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court sale
  • Turn the Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Livingston Parish? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Livingston Parish houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Fees

Selling in Livingston Parish?
We buy Livingston Parish houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Clerk address/hours not seen
  • Sheriff interest text from news article only

What does the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court do when a house sells?

The clerk is the parish recorder: deeds, mortgages and other property papers become public record at the clerk's recording desk. Louisiana counties are called parishes, and in Livingston Parish that office is the one buyers, sellers, title companies and heirs all end up dealing with.

When a document arrives, a deputy clerk stamps it with a unique instrument number and an index book and page number. The stamp also records the date, hour and minute of filing.

Under Civil Code article 3346, an instrument that creates or relates to a mortgage or privilege on land goes into the mortgage records of the parish. Every other instrument, including an act of sale, goes into the conveyance records. A single closing in Livingston Parish can therefore put papers into both sets of books.

Where is the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court office and when is it open?

The main office is at 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754, with a mailing address of P. O. Box 1150. The phone number listed on the clerk's locations page is 225-686-2216 and the fax is 225-686-1867.

A satellite office is listed in Denham Springs at 145 Del Orleans Avenue, Bldg. 2, Suite E, 70726. We could not confirm which services, including recording, are handled at the satellite, so call before driving there with a deed.

The hours page gives office hours as Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Closings that fall near these dates should be planned around the holiday list for 2026:

  • Tuesday, November 3 (General Election Day)
  • Wednesday, November 11 (Veterans' Day)
  • Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving and the day after)
  • Thursday, December 24, Friday, December 25 and Thursday, December 31

How much does it cost to record a deed in Livingston Parish?

Recording a deed or mortgage of one to five pages costs $125 under the clerk's posted schedule. Longer documents cost more, and a few extras apply to indexing and to papers that are formatted wrongly.

ItemFee on the clerk's schedule
Recording, pages 1 to 5$125.00
Recording, pages 6 to 25$225.00
Recording, pages 26 to 50$325.00
Indexing, first ten names per bookIncluded
Each additional name per book$5
Copies, per page$1.00
Certified copy$10.00
Conformed copy$5.00
Cancellation of mortgage, original note$35.00
Cancellation with affidavit$75.00

These figures come from the fee page, which the clerk's site last modified in December 2025. Confirm the current total with the office before closing, because a legislature or a clerk can change a schedule at any time.

Is there a transfer tax when a house is recorded in Livingston Parish?

The clerk's fee schedule shows recording, indexing, copy, map and cancellation charges, and it lists no per-dollar transfer tax line. We could not find a separate parish transfer tax on the clerk's pages, so treat the schedule above as the clerk's side of the cost and ask the closing attorney or title company for the full settlement figures.

The distinction matters to sellers who expect a percentage-based charge at the clerk's counter. What the clerk collects is a fee for handling pages and names. Other closing items, such as payoff of a mortgage or unpaid property tax, are handled between the parties and the title company.

What format must a deed follow so the Livingston clerk will accept it cleanly?

The recording desk says Louisiana statutes set the format, and a document that misses it can draw an extra $10 noncompliance fee. The clerk quotes R.S. 13:844(D)(1): the document must be captioned by type of act on the first page, with a two inch margin at the top, a one inch margin at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than eight point.

Multiple indebtedness mortgages carry the same format rule under R.S. 9:5217(B). A short checklist before sending a deed to the clerk:

  • Caption the first page with the type of act.
  • Leave the margins described above.
  • Use type of eight point or larger.
  • Do not expect the original back, because the clerk's page states that originals are not returned and become part of the parish archives.

If you want proof of what you filed, the filing party can ask for a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at the time of filing.

How do mortgage certificates and mortgage cancellations work here?

The mortgage section issues certificates and cancels mortgage inscriptions, and both start with a written request. Louisiana law requires certificate requests to be in writing, and the office accepts them by fax as well. You must name the exact people to check and supply a legal property description.

The clerk is careful to say a mortgage certificate, properly called a certificate of non-mortgage, is not a title opinion and says nothing about who owns the property. It lists what is recorded against the names searched.

On cancellations, the clerk's page states that since July 1, 2006, a borrower who pays off a mortgage on Livingston Parish real estate is responsible for making sure the mortgage is cancelled. The office requires the original note marked "paid" on its face and will not accept faxes or copies. If the note was lost, the page points the owner back to the lender, and it explains that lost note affidavits have mostly been replaced under R.S. 44:109 by an authentic act from a licensed financial institution.

For a seller, an old mortgage that was paid years ago but never cancelled can surface late in a sale. Checking the mortgage records early gives time to fix it.

How can a seller research a Livingston Parish property's records?

The conveyance section lets the public research property transactions, mineral leases, restrictions and subdivision maps through written or computerized indexes that date back to 1875. Large-screen computer stations are available for real estate agents, surveyors, appraisers, abstractors and attorneys, and staff help is free.

Surveys are a common stumbling block. The clerk notes Louisiana law does not require a survey of conveyed property to be recorded or separately indexed, so some surveys were never recorded or cannot be retrieved. The mapping section keeps a map index showing for whom a map was prepared, the property size, its location and the surveyor, and staff say a surveyor may hold a copy when the clerk does not.

For ownership lines, the clerk points to the parish ownership map on the assessor's website, livingstonassessor.com.

What is Livingston Parish like for a home seller?

Livingston Parish sits east of Baton Rouge, and the Greater Baton Rouge Economic Partnership profile lists Denham Springs, Walker, Livingston, Albany and Springfield as its cities and towns. Wikipedia's list adds Watson as an unincorporated census-designated place and names Livingston as the parish seat, so the main clerk's office sits in the town of Livingston.

The same profile calls it one of the fastest-growing parishes in Louisiana, with an annualized growth rate of 1.64 percent, and credits Interstate 12 for east-west access. It describes construction, distribution and retail as the parish's well-known sectors, and it names Northshore Technical Community College and Livingston Parish Public Schools as workforce and education anchors. The profile says the school district earned an "A" rating from the Louisiana Department of Education.

Watson, in the northwest part of the parish, sits around Range Road (LA 16) and Springfield Road (LA 1019), about 6 miles north of Denham Springs along LA 16.

How did the 2016 flood change selling a house in Livingston Parish?

The August 2016 flood is still part of nearly every house conversation in the parish. A state economic impact report estimated that 38,300 of Livingston Parish's 52,104 housing units flooded, and named East Baton Rouge and Livingston as the hardest hit parishes. The National Weather Service gauge page for the Amite River at Denham Springs lists August 14, 2016 as the flood of record.

For sellers this shows up in three ways:

  • Buyers and lenders ask whether a house took water, what was rebuilt and who did the work.
  • Elevation, flood zone and insurance history become part of price talks.
  • Records of repairs, permits and contractor payments help answer those questions.

A flood-history house that still needs work is a common reason owners look at an as-is sale instead of a repair and listing route.

What should heirs or owners with a distressed Livingston Parish house check first?

Start with the recorded history: pull the conveyance records for the last transfer, then the mortgage records for open liens. A clean record of who owns the house and what is owed makes any sale, cash or otherwise, move faster.

If the owner died, the paperwork that moves title to heirs is a court or affidavit process described on our Louisiana estate tax guide, and it ends with a document that eventually goes to the same recording desk. For rented houses, see our guides on the eviction process and the eviction notice.

More questions about Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Livingston Parish?

At the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court's recording desk, 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754. A Denham Springs satellite office is also listed, but confirm by phone that it takes recordings. The main number is 225-686-2216.

How much is the recording fee for a short deed in Livingston Parish?

The clerk's schedule lists $125 for pages 1 to 5, $225 for pages 6 to 25 and $325 for pages 26 to 50, with the first ten names per book included in indexing. Check with the office for the current total.

Does the Livingston Parish clerk return the original deed?

No. The clerk's page says original documents are not returned and become part of the parish archives. You can request a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at filing.

Who cancels a paid-off mortgage in Livingston Parish?

The borrower is responsible. The clerk says that since July 1, 2006, it is the borrower, not the lender, who may be hurt if a paid mortgage is not cancelled, and the office needs the original note marked paid.

Is a mortgage certificate the same as a title opinion?

No. The clerk states that a certificate of non-mortgage is not a title opinion and makes no representation about who owns the property.

Can I sell a flood-damaged Livingston Parish house as-is?

Yes, owners can sell as-is, but expect buyers to ask for repair, permit and insurance history. Get your recorded title and mortgage payoff in order first so the record does not slow the sale.
